title: Piper Aircraft Co. v. Reyno (1981)
summary: The less favorable law available in Scotland did not bar dismissal when the Scottish accident and parties made that forum more appropriate.
notes:
Forum non conveniens dismisses in favor of another system; § 1404 transfers within the federal system. A foreign forum still must be available and adequate, and conditions on dismissal can matter.

The 1976 crash killed the pilot and five Scottish passengers; Piper built the plane in Pennsylvania and Hartzell Propeller built the propeller in Ohio; Gaynell Reyno, a California legal secretary appointed administratrix, filed in California state court, and the case was removed and then transferred under § 1404(a) to the Middle District of Pennsylvania.

Rule statements: a foreign plaintiff's choice of a United States forum deserves less deference than a resident's, and an unfavorable change in law may be given substantial weight only where the alternative forum's remedy is so clearly inadequate or unsatisfactory that it is no remedy at all; the district court's balancing of the Gilbert private- and public-interest factors is reviewed for abuse of discretion.

sections.Parties: Reyno, appointed representative of the deceased passengers’ estates, sued Piper Aircraft and Hartzell Propeller. The victims and accident were connected to Scotland; the manufacturers were American.
sections.Material Facts: A small aircraft crashed in Scotland, killing Scottish passengers. The aircraft and propeller were manufactured in the United States, while the operator, maintenance circumstances, accident investigation, wreckage, and many witnesses were in Britain. The action was initiated through a representative in California and sought the advantages of American liability law. Scotland offered a forum, although its law was less favorable to the plaintiffs, including in its treatment of strict liability. The defendants agreed to conditions enabling the Scottish litigation.
sections.Procedural History: The action was removed and transferred to federal court in Pennsylvania. The district court dismissed on forum non conveniens grounds. The court of appeals reversed, emphasizing the unfavorable change in law. The Supreme Court reversed the appellate court and sustained the discretionary dismissal framework.
sections.Issue: Does a less favorable foreign substantive law prevent forum non conveniens dismissal, and did the district court properly weigh the competing interests?
sections.Holding: An unfavorable change in law ordinarily does not bar dismissal. The district court’s balance of the private and public factors was permissible on this record.
sections.Reasoning: If a plaintiff could defeat dismissal simply by identifying more favorable forum law, the doctrine would have little practical force. An alternative forum may be inadequate where it offers no meaningful remedy, but a difference in the level or theory of recovery is not ordinarily enough. The Court also considered access to proof, witnesses, the ability to involve other responsible parties, and the local interest in resolving a local accident. A foreign representative’s selection of an American forum did not carry the same inference of convenience as a resident’s choice. Those considerations supported Scotland despite the American manufacture of the components. The district court’s task was to balance the actual litigation difficulties rather than decide which jurisdiction had the most generous law.

learning.why: The less favorable law available in Scotland did not bar dismissal when the Scottish accident and parties made that forum more appropriate.

topics.cp-forum-non-conveniens: The court could dismiss in favor of a substantially more appropriate foreign forum after weighing private and public interests. Less favorable substantive law did not automatically make Scotland inadequate.
topics.cp-venue: A foreign plaintiff’s forum choice received less deference because convenience was less readily inferred.
topics.cp-supplemental-discretion: The discretionary balance had to rest on the actual evidence, parties, and locations.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Piper describes forum non conveniens as a discretionary balancing of private and public interests and applies deferential review to the district court’s supported choice.
topics.cp-transfer: The case reached Pennsylvania by § 1404(a) transfer, and the Court's Van Dusen discussion explains why transfer would not fix the choice-of-law problem.
topics.cp-forum-shopping: Reyno admitted she sued in the United States for its more favorable law, and the Court's reduced deference to foreign plaintiffs is aimed at that forum shopping.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Marshall wrote for the Court. Justice White concurred in part and dissented in part, and Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Brennan, dissented, agreeing that an unfavorable change in law is not dispositive but arguing the Court should have vacated and remanded for the Third Circuit to review the district court's balancing. Justices Powell and O'Connor took no part.

mnemonic.rationale: A crash in the Scottish highlands
